results.authors: Louis DN, Perry A, Wesseling P, et al.
results.summary: The 2021 WHO CNS tumor classification integrates molecular parameters into the diagnostic criteria. Glioblastoma is defined as an IDH-wildtype diffuse glioma with at least one of: microvascular proliferation, necrosis, EGFR amplification, whole chromosome 7 gain/10 loss, or TERT promoter mutation. IDH-wildtype tumors meeting these criteria are classified as WHO grade 4 regardless of histologic grade. IDH-mutant tumors with similar histology are reclassified as astrocytoma IDH-mutant.
results.title: The 2021 WHO classification of tumors of the central nervous system: a summary

results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.summary: Landmark phase III trial establishing the Stupp protocol: maximal safe resection followed by fractionated radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with concurrent daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2), then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, days 1-5 of 28-day cycle). Median overall survival improved from 12.1 to 14.6 months. MGMT methylation was a strong prognostic and predictive biomarker.
results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma

results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.summary: Elevated rCBV ratios (>1.75) on perfusion MRI and elevated Cho/NAA ratios on MR spectroscopy are reliable indicators of high-grade glioma (WHO grades 3-4). Combined use improves sensitivity and specificity for grading compared to conventional MRI alone.
results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy

differential.key_features: No known primary malignancy; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative FLAIR edema along white matter tracts and optic radiation involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis

Immunocompetent patient; PCNSL typically presents as a homogeneously enhancing periventricular or deep gray matter mass with diffuse central DWI restriction; ring enhancement with central necrosis and elevated rCBV argue against lymphoma

Mildly elevated CRP and ESR could suggest infection, but absent fever, normal WBC, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus), and markedly elevated rCBV are inconsistent with pyogenic abscess

Age, sex, absence of prior demyelinating events, thick closed ring enhancement rather than open-ring, central necrosis, and markedly elevated rCBV and Cho/NAA all argue strongly against tumefactive MS

Progressive three-week course with worsening mass effect, thick irregular ring enhancement, and markedly elevated rCBV are incompatible with infarction; MRI restricted diffusion is at the tumor rim rather than vascular territory distribution

key_clinical_evidence: Progressive subacute aphasia (non-fluent output, impaired comprehension and repetition) with morning headaches and a right superior quadrantanopia in a 64-year-old man localizes to the left temporal lobe and strongly mandates urgent contrast-enhanced MRI to exclude a structural mass

MRI demonstrating a large left temporal ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, restricted diffusion at the rim, perilesional FLAIR edema involving the optic radiation, and mild midline shift is characteristic of high-grade glioma; the optic radiation FLAIR signal explains the right superior quadrantanopia

Mildly elevated ESR (42 mm/hr) and CRP (7.8 mg/L) may prompt consideration of an infectious or inflammatory etiology (abscess, tumefactive MS), but no fever, no leukocytosis, thick irregular ring enhancement with necrosis, and markedly elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess or demyelination
Perfusion MRI (markedly elevated rCBV ratio 4.3) and MR spectroscopy (Cho/Cr 4.0, NAA/Cr 0.3, lipid-lactate peaks) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help direct biopsy to the highest-grade region

The left temporal location involves language-eloquent cortex (Wernicke's area, superior and middle temporal gyri); neurosurgical planning should include awake craniotomy with language mapping to maximize extent of resection while preserving language function
Tissue diagnosis with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, TERT, EGFR, 1p/19q) is mandatory before definitive treatment; imaging alone cannot distinguish glioblastoma from other high-grade neoplasms

For IDH-wildtype GBM, standard treatment is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent RT + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide); MGMT methylation predicts improved benefit from temozolomide

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Washington is a 64-year-old right-handed African American man and retired high school history teacher who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a three-week history of progressive language dysfunction. His wife first noticed that he was pausing more during conversation approximately 21 days ago, initially attributing this to fatigue. Over the following week, the pauses became more frequent and he began substituting incorrect words, occasionally using completely unrelated words in sentences. He reported difficulty understanding his wife when she spoke more than a few words at a time, which he described as 'people are speaking too fast.' Over the past ten days, he has developed worsening headaches, predominantly left-sided and temporal in location, worst in the morning and partially responsive to acetaminophen. His wife reports that he has seemed more forgetful over the past week, missing two tutoring appointments and repeatedly asking the same questions within short intervals. Two days prior to admission, he had a 30-second episode of complete speech arrest with preservation of consciousness, witnessed by his wife, after which he reported a brief throbbing headache. He also reports intermittent blurring in the upper right portion of his visual field, which his wife describes as him bumping into objects on his right side. He has had one episode of nausea without vomiting, occurring in the morning three days ago. He denies any prior episodes of speech difficulty, prior seizures, head trauma, fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss. He has no history of malignancy and no recent travel outside the continental United States. Initial brain MRI with contrast performed in the outpatient setting one week ago was reported as demonstrating an abnormal lesion in the left temporal lobe with surrounding signal abnormality; he was referred urgently to neurology for inpatient evaluation. Repeat MRI on admission confirms a large left temporal heterogeneously enhancing mass. He was admitted for further evaluation and was started on dexamethasone for symptom management.
